context: Current closing price of Electronic Arts (EA): $203.02 USD as of 2026-06-17.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assumed was a recent trading price near $203, with very little directional conviction. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price because short-term mean reversion and liquidity dynamics tend to keep prices near their last close absent a specific catalyst. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to around $204, reflecting a small positive drift assumption consistent with the long-run equity risk premium but acknowledging that a week is too short for that drift to matter much statistically. At the one-month horizon, I moved the estimate modestly to $205, again reflecting only a marginal expected drift. In all three cases, the point estimates are essentially "near current price with a small positive tilt," which is the rational default when no strong directional signal is present.

The confidence interval widths were driven primarily by the time scaling of volatility. Equity prices typically exhibit volatility in the range of 15–25% annualized, and scaling that to one day, one week, and one month produces progressively wider intervals. The one-day interval of roughly plus or minus $5.5 around the estimate reflects realized daily volatility for a typical large-cap or index-like instrument. The one-week interval expands to roughly plus or minus $10, and the one-month interval widens further to plus or minus $20, consistent with the square-root-of-time rule for uncertainty accumulation. I also incorporated a modest fat-tail adjustment, meaning I widened the intervals slightly beyond what a pure normal distribution would suggest, because financial returns are known to have heavier tails than the Gaussian model predicts.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise macro shock — such as an unexpected Federal Reserve policy shift, a significant geopolitical escalation, or a sudden credit event — could easily produce a move of 10% or more even within a single week, which would breach the lower bound of my one-week interval. Earnings announcements or guidance from major index constituents could also produce outsized moves if results dramatically miss or beat expectations. On the upside, a sudden easing of financial conditions, a positive resolution to a geopolitical risk, or a stronger-than-expected economic data release could push prices beyond the upper bounds. My intervals implicitly assume no single catastrophic or euphoric event, and the real world regularly produces exactly those kinds of events, meaning the true tails are fatter than even my adjusted intervals imply.
